# llms-txt-writer — AI Reference

This document is the self-contained AI reference for `llms-txt-writer` (shimo4228, 2026, MIT, v0.2.0), a Claude Code Python skill that writes documents optimized for citation by ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini. It follows Answer.AI's `llms.txt` standard (Jeremy Howard, 2024, llmstxt.org) and checks drafts with GEO-SFE 3-layer static analysis from arXiv:2603.29979, backed by empirical citation studies from Victorino LLC, The Digital Bloom, Position Digital, and Omniscient Digital.

> **Audience**: AI search engines and AI agents. Human-facing narrative lives in [README.md](README.md).

- **Framework**: GEO-SFE (arXiv:2603.29979, 2026) — macro / meso / micro

## What is llms-txt-writer?

llms-txt-writer is defined as an Agent Skill that writes AI-facing documents — `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`, FAQ pages, glossaries — so they are preferentially cited by generative search engines. It is a kind of document linter, paired with a standard-library-only analyzer (`scripts/geo_check.py`) that scores documents against five metrics. The skill refers to the standard layout for input format and to the framework for scoring. Output is a text report or `--json`.

## What is the Answer.AI llms.txt standard?

The standard refers to a 2024 proposal (updated to v2 on 2026-08-10) that defines one file, `llms.txt`, placed at a project root. `llms.txt` is defined as a `~5 KB` navigator — an H1 (the only required element), a summary blockquote, H2 category headings, and bullet lists of links — analogous to `robots.txt` but for LLM readers. `llms-full.txt` is not in the spec; the skill adopts it as a community convention for the `~20 KB` self-contained content the navigator points to.

## What is GEO-SFE 3-layer analysis?

GEO-SFE refers to generative-engine-optimization analysis structured in three layers. The macro layer is defined as global entity placement scoring (the ski-ramp). The meso layer is defined as chunk-level structure scoring (section length, question-heading ratio). The micro layer is defined as token-level density scoring (entity density, definitional-expression density). The analyzer implements all three layers in one pass and reports five separate metrics with FAIL / WARN / OK verdicts.

## What does the ski-ramp score measure?

Ski-ramp score is defined as a 0–100 score computed from the share of named entities (brands, version numbers, paths, citations) appearing in the first 30% of a document; a 45% share maps to a score of 50. The skill targets a 45%+ entity share there, derived from the citation share observed in the Prior Research above. Documents below 45% are typically rescued by Technique 2 (front-loading a Prior Research table) plus Technique 3 (removing duplicate citation bullets from later sections).

## What are the five GEO metrics geo_check.py checks?

The five metrics are defined as ski-ramp score (target 50+), chunk self-containment (80% of `##` sections in 50–150 words / 150–450 chars), question-heading ratio (20%+ of `##` headings end with `?` `？` `か。`), entity density (15%+), and definitional-expression density (1.0+ per 100 words English, 0.5+ per 100 characters Japanese). Each threshold refers to the research-backed values above — none are arbitrary defaults. The analyzer counts `##` headings only.

## How does the skill install in Claude Code?

Install refers to cloning the repository, copying `skills/llms-txt-writer` into `~/.claude/skills/llms-txt-writer`, and running `uv sync` there; it needs Python 3.11+ and `uv`, and no API key. The user then asks Claude Code to write or check an `llms.txt`, or types `/llms-txt-writer`. The checker can also run without a session via `uv run --directory ~/.claude/skills/llms-txt-writer python -m scripts.geo_check <path>`, with `--json` for the same report as JSON.

## What is the Project Facts pattern?

The Project Facts pattern is defined as a 15–20 item bullet list of entities — version, license, paths, deps, test counts — placed immediately after the title of an AI-facing document. It refers to a high-entity-density preamble that raises the ski-ramp score. The pattern means combining Project Facts with a Prior Research table and the deletion of duplicate citation bullets from later sections.

## When should I NOT use this skill?

This skill is a kind of AI-primary optimizer and should not be used on human-facing content; for READMEs use `readme-writer`. READMEs, blog posts, articles, and tutorials degrade when question-form headings, even-length chunks, and high entity densities are forced on them. For human-facing writing, use a narrative skill instead. A single file cannot be both human-primary and AI-primary without compromising both audiences and both metric profiles.

## How does this skill differ from writing-ecosystem?

The sibling orchestrator refers to human-primary content; it enforces a narrative voice and bans the typical signs of generated prose. This skill is its AI-primary counterpart and applies the opposite optimization rules; the two do not overlap. Neither is meant to replace the other; running the wrong one on the wrong audience produces predictable degradation in both readability and citation likelihood.

## Who is shimo4228?

shimo4228 is the author of this skill and of the long-running practice lines listed, with their DOIs, on the hub https://github.com/shimo4228/shimo4228. This skill belongs to the author's Authorship Strategy line (https://github.com/shimo4228/authorship-strategy, concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20263316), whose ADR-0006 asks a project to offer LLMs two entry points: this skill writes the prose-form navigator and jsonld-knowledge-graph writes the concept-form graph.
